title: Reading test 1 · Cities, objects & sound
description: Original 40-question Academic Reading simulation: three fictional passages, 60 minutes. Difficulty is not calibrated to an IELTS band. Answer only from the texts. The timer starts when you open a new test; pausing makes it an untimed practice attempt. The clock submits all answers, including blanks, when time expires.
passage:
A. In the fictional city of Merrow, a university seed store had occupied the basement of a municipal building for nearly forty years. Its earliest collection consisted mainly of vegetables grown in neighbouring farms, and each packet carried the name of the person who had donated it. Over time, the store also received seeds from derelict railway land, small gardens and the edges of drainage channels. These arrivals changed its purpose. The director, Hana Voss, argued that saving useful crop varieties remained important, but that the city also needed a record of plants adapting to its changing streets. Her proposal was to collect more widely rather than replace the agricultural collection.

B. The new collecting scheme recruited residents to identify possible sites. Volunteers were not asked to choose plants simply because they looked unusual. Instead, they photographed the whole site, recorded its position and described the conditions in which each plant grew. A narrow strip beside a warm factory wall could offer different conditions from a shaded courtyard only a few metres away. Staff checked these records before granting permission for seeds to be collected. The system reduced unnecessary disturbance and helped the team avoid collecting repeatedly from the most accessible places. It did not give volunteers authority to enter private land or to remove protected plants.

C. Storage created a less visible difficulty. Seeds that survive drying can often be kept in cold conditions for long periods, but not every species responds to that treatment. The team therefore divided each accepted collection into several small batches. One batch was tested immediately, while others were stored under different conditions. Staff used germination tests to estimate how many seeds could still produce seedlings. An apparently intact packet was not sufficient evidence of a living collection. Some batches were tested more frequently than others because earlier observations suggested a faster loss of viability. There was no single inspection interval for the entire store.

D. The labels proved almost as valuable as the packets. A seed from a dry roadside and a seed of the same species from a damp garden might look identical. Without the collecting records, however, a researcher could not reliably reconstruct the environment in which either had developed. Old donation labels often lacked precise locations, and the team resisted the temptation to supply a confident modern address. It preserved the original wording and added a separate note explaining any uncertainty. Voss described an honest gap as preferable to an invented coordinate that future researchers might treat as measured fact.

E. Public interest rose when the store opened a small demonstration garden. Staff planted selected samples in raised beds and placed their collection histories beside them. Visitors could compare plants associated with different parts of Merrow, but the garden was not a controlled experiment. Soil, watering and shade differed among beds, and there were too few plants to distinguish inherited differences from chance. The signs therefore avoided claiming that a taller plant had genetically adapted to a particular street. The garden's purpose was to explain questions the collection could help researchers ask, rather than announce answers that had not yet been established.

F. Funding decisions brought a different dispute. A sponsor offered to pay for a large number of additional packets, provided that the project reported its success mainly as the number stored. The team declined that condition. Counting packets was straightforward, but a packet without reliable records or viable seeds contributed little to the collection's research value. The revised budget prioritised testing, staff training and improvements to the database before expansion. This choice meant accepting fewer new collections in the following year. It also meant that the store could explain more clearly what it already held and which materials urgently needed attention.

G. The project now shares descriptions of its holdings with other regional stores, although the seeds themselves remain in Merrow. Researchers can request small samples after explaining how the work will use them. Requests are checked against the amount of material available, so approval is not automatic. The next planned study will compare samples from sites that have recently become hotter with samples from similar sites that have changed less. Voss stresses that the store cannot conserve an entire city ecosystem inside a building. Its more limited contribution is to preserve material and records that would otherwise disappear before anyone had an opportunity to study them.

A. When the fictional town of Bellwick converted an unused shop into a repair library, the name caused some confusion. The service did lend tools, but its organisers wanted to provide something beyond access to equipment. A resident might borrow a drill without knowing whether a damaged shelf could safely be fixed. Another might understand the fault but lack the confidence to begin. The library therefore combined loans with advice sessions and small supervised workshops. Its opening leaflet promised a place to investigate repair options, not a guarantee that every broken object could or should be restored.

B. The first lending catalogue had been assembled from donated equipment. This kept the purchase bill low but created a mixture of brands, missing attachments and unfamiliar controls. Before the public opening, volunteers tested each item and wrote a simple operating card. Tools that could not be checked adequately were withheld, even when they appeared almost new. The library then standardised some frequently borrowed items so that a person who had learned to use one version would not encounter an entirely different control layout on the next visit. Variety remained useful, but it was no longer treated as an advantage in itself.

C. The loan records initially appeared to offer an obvious measure of demand: the most frequently borrowed tool must be the one residents needed most. Coordinator Laila Penn questioned that conclusion. Several users had requested a tile cutter, discovered that the only one was unavailable and left without making a reservation. Their unmet requests were absent from the borrowing totals. Conversely, a light vacuum cleaner generated many short loans because it was easy to carry home. The team added a request log, including unsuccessful requests, before deciding what to buy. The new log did not eliminate uncertainty, but it made one source of missing information visible.

D. Advice sessions revealed another distinction. At a public demonstration, a skilled repairer could replace a cable quickly while an audience watched. Visitors often praised the event, yet later interviews found that some could not repeat the procedure themselves. Workshops were redesigned to let participants practise one step on an unplugged training device before attempting the complete task. Tutors also asked learners to explain why a step was necessary. Attendance fell slightly because the smaller groups required advance booking. The organisers accepted that reduction rather than returning to a format that reached more people but provided less opportunity for direct practice.

E. Claims about waste prevention required particular care. A repaired kettle might remain in use, be stored in a cupboard or be replaced soon afterwards. Counting every completed repair as one avoided purchase would therefore overstate what the library knew. A follow-up survey asked whether the object was still being used and whether a replacement had actually been planned. Responses were voluntary, so satisfied users might be more likely to reply. The team reported the response rate beside the results and did not assume that non-respondents behaved in the same way. It also distinguished repair activity from verified changes in purchasing.

F. The library's financial review compared two options for the following year: longer opening hours or more trained advisers. Longer hours might increase access for shift workers, but the existing evening sessions already had queues for individual advice. A short pilot added an adviser to one evening while keeping the hours unchanged. Waiting times decreased, although the pilot was too brief to reveal whether demand would change over a full year. The committee funded additional adviser training first and postponed a permanent extension of the opening schedule. It described this as a response to the available evidence, not a finding that longer hours could never be useful.

G. A final question concerned the role of local repair businesses. Some shop owners feared that a publicly supported library would compete with them. Penn replied that the library referred complex or hazardous work to professionals and made those limits explicit. It did not charge for undertaking repairs on behalf of residents, because that was not the service it offered. Several businesses later helped produce guidance on recognising faults that required specialist attention. The arrangement did not remove every disagreement about public funding, but it weakened the assumption that all forms of repair support were interchangeable. The library's contribution lay in helping residents make better decisions, including the decision to seek paid expertise.

A. In a fictional study at the Halen Marsh Research Station, ecologists tested whether sound recordings could help them monitor changes across a large wetland. Walking surveys remained important, but observers could reach only a limited number of sites during the brief period around dawn. Small recorders could operate at several places simultaneously and preserve material for later inspection. The team did not expect recordings to provide a complete inventory of life. Silent animals would be missed, and an identifiable call might travel far beyond the location of the animal producing it. Sound was a source of evidence with its own blind spots, rather than a substitute for every other method.

B. Choosing recording positions involved a trade-off. Sites beside the main path were easy to visit when batteries needed replacing, but they also captured footsteps, maintenance vehicles and conversations. More distant sites reduced some of that disturbance while increasing travel time and the risk that an equipment fault would remain unnoticed. The team chose a mixture of accessible and remote sites, recording the distance from paths and water at each one. It also mounted the devices at a common height. This did not make the sites identical, but it reduced one avoidable difference in how the microphones received nearby sounds.

C. The first analysis used software to count sound events that resembled bird calls. Researchers initially expected the busiest recordings to indicate the greatest variety of birds. Inspection of selected clips challenged that expectation: one loud species could call repeatedly and dominate a recording containing few other species. The number of detected events and the number of species were therefore different quantities. The team began comparing a sample of automated detections with identifications made by trained listeners. It retained the event counts but stopped describing them as a direct measure of biodiversity. A convenient number could be useful without supporting the strongest interpretation attached to it.

D. Weather complicated the comparison further. Heavy rain masked faint calls, while wind moving reeds created sounds that the software sometimes classified incorrectly. Simply deleting all wet or windy recordings would have produced a quieter dataset, but it would also have removed information about conditions the marsh regularly experienced. Instead, the researchers attached weather notes to each recording period and analysed some conditions separately. They also kept a record of excluded clips and the reason for each exclusion. Another team could then see whether an apparent seasonal difference might partly reflect different amounts of usable material rather than a change in animal activity.

E. A planned maintenance closure created an opportunity to investigate visitor disturbance. One path would be closed for three weeks, and the researchers proposed comparing recordings before, during and after the closure. A fall in human noise would not by itself prove that birds had become more numerous. Animals might change when they called, and quieter conditions could make existing calls easier to detect. The study therefore included nearby paths that remained open as comparison sites. Even then, the closure had not been randomly assigned, so unusual features of that path could influence the result. The researchers treated the comparison as informative but not decisive.

F. An unexpected issue arose when a reviewer asked to inspect the raw recordings. Some clips included intelligible conversations by visitors who had not agreed to take part in research. Publishing all the audio without restriction would have exposed material unrelated to the ecological questions. The station prepared a public collection of approved clips and summary measurements, while requests for other recordings were reviewed under a controlled access procedure. The researchers documented where clips had been removed and why. They argued that useful transparency meant making the methods and limitations inspectable, not ignoring the privacy interests of people who happened to pass a microphone.

G. By the end of the pilot, the team had a more modest but clearer goal. Rather than rank the entire marsh with a single acoustic score, it would track several specified measures over repeated visits. These included the presence of selected call types, the amount of recorded human noise and the proportion of clips suitable for analysis. Periodic walking surveys would provide a separate check on the interpretation. More equipment was not the immediate priority: the station planned to improve annotation, meaning the descriptive labels attached to clips, and test the consistency of different listeners first. Its central lesson was that a larger archive only improves knowledge when researchers understand how its records were produced and what their measurements can legitimately claim.

For many years, guides used it to tell a simple story: Renn installed a public clock and the town immediately began to keep accurate time. A recent exhibition offers a more complicated account. The notebook records repairs, disagreements and periods when the clock was out of service. Its interest lies less in the arrival of a single machine than in the work required to make a shared time signal useful. The exhibition does not claim that the notebook represents every harbour town or every resident's experience.

B. Before the installation, several clocks were already visible around Norhaven. The church clock was prominent, while workshops and shipping offices owned smaller ones. Their displayed times did not always agree. This was inconvenient when a customer arrived for an appointment, but especially troublesome when workers had to coordinate loading with a departing vessel. Renn's first proposal did not require the destruction of those clocks. He suggested a harbour clock whose daily signal could be used to adjust them. Agreement depended on people accepting a common reference, rather than on every household buying an equally precise instrument.

C. Finding a suitable location proved difficult. A tower near the market would be easy for pedestrians to see but was partly hidden from the quays by warehouses. A position at the outer harbour offered better visibility to ships, although strong winds and salt spray would make maintenance harder. The committee eventually chose a roof above the customs office. Its decision reflected several requirements at once: visibility from the working harbour, access for the person winding the mechanism and the strength of the existing structure. It was a compromise rather than a location that maximised every advantage independently.

D. The first month produced complaints that the new clock was unreliable. Some were justified: the notebook records a loose component and a temporary stoppage. Others arose because observers compared the dial with different references and assumed their own familiar clock must be correct. Renn began keeping a daily adjustment record, noting the reference used and the amount of any correction. This made disagreement easier to investigate. It did not mean that the public clock never drifted again. The exhibition shows that reliability depended partly on a documented process for detecting and correcting errors, not merely on confidence in a well-made mechanism.

E. Visibility alone did not solve the problem for people working inside sheds. The committee added a bell at midday, allowing a time signal to reach those who could not see the dial. Yet visitors should not imagine that the bell was equally audible everywhere. Loading machinery and distance affected what could be heard. Nor did everyone want the same signal schedule. Shopkeepers asked for additional strikes during the afternoon, whereas some nearby residents objected to the noise. Surviving minutes record those requests, but no decision on extra strikes has been found. The museum leaves that question open instead of supplying an attractive ending.

F. Payment for the service was another continuing issue. The shipping association contributed to installation but argued that the town should cover routine upkeep. The council regarded the harbour businesses as the main beneficiaries and proposed an annual contribution from them. A breakdown during a busy week exposed the weakness of an arrangement with no agreed maintenance budget. A later contract paid Renn a fixed yearly sum to inspect and service the clock, while major replacement parts required separate approval. The contract did not transfer ownership of the clock to Renn. It established responsibilities that the original purchase had left uncertain.

G. The exhibition closes with two kinds of evidence: Renn's adjustment pages and workers' recollections recorded many years later. The first offers precise entries about particular interventions, but says little about how residents felt. The second describes habits and frustrations, although dates and sequences are not always consistent. Curators resist using either source as a complete account. Together, they show why a public clock can be understood as a social arrangement supported by technical equipment. A machine could display a time; a functioning common standard also required maintenance, agreed references and people willing and able to use its signals.

A. In a fictional trial, a document-processing company called Arlen Services allowed one department to work four days a week for the same weekly pay. The department's scheduled hours fell, and managers promised to evaluate the arrangement after twelve weeks. Newspaper coverage later described the trial as proof that all organisations could reduce hours without losing output. The internal report was more cautious. Its central question was whether this particular department could maintain the quality and timeliness of its work under a revised schedule. The researchers did not design the trial to settle the question for every occupation, and they explicitly separated an interesting local result from a universal recommendation.

B. Before the change, managers usually counted completed cases each week. The researchers added the number returned for correction and the time customers waited for a decision. An employee could close many simple cases while leaving difficult ones unresolved, so volume alone might reward the wrong behaviour. The team also recorded the mix of cases entering the department. A week with unusually straightforward requests could produce a higher total without any improvement in the process. Recording several measures made the report less convenient to summarise in a headline, but it reduced the risk that one attractive figure would hide deterioration elsewhere.

C. The department changed more than its timetable. Routine meetings were shortened, staff were given protected periods for uninterrupted work, and a shared checklist replaced several repeated email exchanges. Some employees welcomed the changes, while others said that compressed deadlines made the remaining days feel more intense. Because these changes occurred together, an improvement could not be attributed to the shorter week alone. The report described the trial as a package of organisational changes. It recommended a later comparison that varied the meeting rules separately, rather than assuming that any employer adopting four working days would obtain the same result without changing how work was organised.

D. A nearby department kept its usual schedule and supplied comparison data. This was useful because a company-wide software outage affected both departments in the sixth week. Looking only at the trial department might have made that temporary fall in output appear to be caused by the new timetable. However, the two departments did not receive identical work, and staff had not been randomly allocated between them. The comparison could help interpret shared events without removing every alternative explanation. The researchers retained the outage week in the main results and also showed calculations excluding it, explaining the reason for the additional analysis.

E. Employee wellbeing was measured through short voluntary questionnaires at the start, middle and end of the trial. The final responses were generally more positive about time available outside work. Yet some employees did not answer the last questionnaire, including several who had taken leave. The researchers did not know whether those missing responses would have been more positive or more negative. They therefore reported participation numbers and matched responses from the same people where possible. Anonymous comments offered examples of personal experiences, but they were not treated as evidence that every member of staff had benefited in an identical way.

F. The twelve-week results showed a similar number of completed cases, fewer recorded corrections and no clear change in typical customer waiting time. Managers considered this sufficient to extend the pilot, but not enough to guarantee permanent adoption. The trial had taken place outside the department's busiest season. A longer observation period would help reveal whether backlogs built up when requests increased, and whether initial enthusiasm faded. The team also wanted to check if work had shifted informally into evenings or days off. Scheduled hours alone could not establish that total hours actually worked had fallen by the same amount.

G. The final report recommended retaining the revised arrangement for another six months while continuing measurement. It did not calculate a single score combining output, customer experience and wellbeing, because doing so would require choices about the relative value of each. Those choices belonged in discussion with staff and customers, not hidden inside an apparently neutral average. The company published the measurement definitions alongside the summary. The researchers hoped that other organisations would borrow the questions and the caution about interpretation, rather than treat the timetable itself as a recipe. A useful trial could narrow uncertainty without removing the need for further evidence.

A. The fictional Esten Museum digitised a collection of excavation notebooks so that researchers could consult them without repeatedly handling fragile pages. The project began with photographs and transcriptions, then added a search interface. Publicity celebrated the fact that a person could now retrieve a word from thousands of pages in seconds. Curator Tomas Iven welcomed the convenience but worried about a misleading impression: a fast search did not turn a collection into a complete account of the past. What could be found depended on what had survived, what had been collected and how the digital descriptions were produced. Each stage introduced its own selections and gaps.

B. The original notebooks themselves were uneven. Some excavators carefully described ordinary objects, while others devoted most of their pages to unusual finds. A missing mention of a cooking pot therefore did not necessarily mean that no pot had been discovered. It might reflect a decision about what was worth recording. Dates and place names also changed between projects, and some pages contained abbreviations that nobody could confidently expand. The digital team retained those uncertain forms rather than converting every entry into a uniform modern description. Researchers could view the photographed page beside the transcription and decide how much confidence to place in a proposed reading.

C. Automatic text recognition accelerated the first draft of the transcription, but its errors were not randomly distributed. It performed better on clear printed headings than on cramped handwritten notes, and damaged corners sometimes produced invented characters. The team used human checking on a sample of pages from different handwriting styles, rather than inspecting only the cleanest scans. It also added confidence flags so that uncertain readings could be found for later review. A page marked as uncertain was still made available; the flag communicated a limitation rather than declaring the entire page worthless. The original image remained the reference when a transcription was disputed.

D. Searching introduced another problem. Someone typing the modern name of a location might receive no results, even when the notebooks contained many entries under an older spelling. The team built a list connecting known variants and offered an optional expanded search. However, similar-looking names could refer to different places. An expansion that automatically merged them might produce a larger but less relevant result list. The interface therefore showed which additional terms had been used and allowed researchers to turn expansion off. The goal was to make the search process inspectable, not simply to maximise the number of apparent matches.

E. Users also asked to sort finds by material. This appeared straightforward until the team encountered entries such as “probably bone” and “wood or darkened leather”. Assigning each to one material category would have removed the original uncertainty. The catalogue instead distinguished confirmed labels from tentative ones and allowed a record to carry more than one possible interpretation. That complicated counting. A researcher estimating the number of wooden objects needed to state whether uncertain records were included. Iven argued that a clean total was not automatically a better total. Its usefulness depended on a definition that another researcher could understand and, if necessary, challenge.

F. A trial with student researchers revealed how the interface affected reading habits. Many participants opened the first relevant-looking result and stopped searching, even when later results contained contradictory information. The team added a short prompt encouraging users to inspect neighbouring pages and check the collection context. It did not force every person through an identical sequence or claim that the prompt had solved the problem. A follow-up study was planned to see whether it changed actual search behaviour. The trial suggested that making material accessible was only one part of helping people use it critically; the design of a convenient route through the material also mattered.

G. Digitisation changed the museum's work rather than finishing it. New transcriptions, corrected links and revised material labels required version records so that a researcher could identify what had been consulted at a particular time. Stable page identifiers were kept even when descriptions changed. The museum also retained its physical notebooks under controlled storage conditions. Digital access reduced some handling, but it did not justify treating the originals as disposable. In the project's final guidance, Iven described the catalogue as a revisable argument about a collection. Its value came from connecting evidence, interpretation and uncertainty in ways that users could inspect, not from making every search result appear equally certain.

title: Research meeting · evidence before conclusions
description: Original listening practice with a computer-generated English voice. Read the questions, listen, then submit to unlock the transcript. Not an official test or a band predictor.
passage:
Tutor: Let us review your project on the new campus bicycle stands. What was your original question? Student: Whether adding stands increased cycling. We counted bicycles beside the library for two weeks before installation and two weeks afterwards. The counts were higher afterwards. Tutor: That is useful, but what else changed? Student: The later period had much drier weather. We should not attribute the whole increase to the stands.

Tutor: Did you count at the same time each day? Student: Yes, at eleven in the morning. We first planned nine, but a delivery vehicle often blocked the view then. The counts were done on weekdays only. We did not collect weekend data. Tutor: Include that limitation. Also distinguish parked bicycles from the number of individual cyclists. A bicycle could remain in the same place for several days.

Student: We also asked students whether they liked the stands. We collected eighty-four questionnaires. Tutor: How did you recruit people? Student: We approached cyclists near the library entrance. Tutor: Then you cannot treat that sample as representative of everyone on campus. You may have missed people who do not cycle because they need stands in another location. Put the recruitment method in the methods section.

Student: For the follow-up, should we buy automatic counters? Tutor: Not yet. First compare another location where no new stands were installed. Keep the observation times the same and record the weather. Use a spreadsheet for the field notes, but keep the original count sheets too. Submit your revised plan by Tuesday. The presentation is on Friday, so those are separate deadlines. In your conclusion, say what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain, rather than claiming that a higher count proves the policy caused more cycling.

title: Urban river lecture · restoration and measurement
description: Original listening practice with a computer-generated English voice. Read the questions, listen, then submit to unlock the transcript. Not an official test or a band predictor.
passage:
Today I will discuss a fictional river-restoration pilot in the town of Elwick. The project removed a concrete channel from a four-hundred-metre stretch of river. Engineers created shallow banks and planted reeds. The work was intended to improve habitat and reduce the speed of water during ordinary high flows. It was not designed to prevent every possible flood.

The first survey took place in April, before construction. A second survey was planned for September but heavy rain delayed it until October. Researchers measured water temperature at five locations. They also recorded the number of visible fish, although they warned that visibility differed between days. Cloudy water made fish harder to count, so a lower count did not necessarily indicate fewer fish.

The team collected water samples every fortnight. Samples were stored in labelled bottles and taken to the laboratory on the same day. A broken instrument meant that nitrate results were unavailable for the first three sampling dates. Those results were marked missing rather than entered as zero. A zero would have claimed a measurement that had never been made.

Local volunteers photographed the river from fixed points. Using the same position helped comparisons, but light and water level still varied. Photographs were stored in a shared archive with dates and weather notes. The project also surveyed residents. Many welcomed the planted banks, while some worried that the area looked untidy. These were opinions about appearance, not direct measurements of habitat quality.

For the next year, the researchers recommended monitoring an upstream comparison stretch that had not been altered. They wanted to distinguish local changes from patterns affecting the river more widely. They also proposed a survey of insects, because fish counts alone could not describe every part of the habitat. Their final report separated engineering aims, ecological observations and public responses. Each offered useful evidence, but none could simply stand in for all the others.
